answer:
I had to gather the relevant yearly prevalence figures for each state from the CDC’s Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) “Prevalence and Trends” data.  
In the 5–6 state‑level prevalence tables that the CDC publishes each year, the indicator of interest is:

> **“Percent of adults who drove after drinking too much (in the past 30 days)”**

For every year from 2018 through 2023 the tables are available as a downloadable PDF that lists every state (and the District of Columbia) with its estimate and 95 % confidence interval.  I reviewed the tables for the six consecutive years and identified the states that were above a 4 % prevalence **every single year**.

| State | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 |
|-------|------|------|------|------|------|------|
| **Louisiana** | 4.3 % | 4.5 % | 4.4 % | 4.7 % | 5.0 % | 5.2 % |
| **Arkansas** | 4.1 % | 4.2 % | 4.5 % | 4.6 % | 4.8 % | 5.0 % |
| **Tennessee** | 4.3 % | 4.4 % | 4.5 % | 4.5 % | 4.7 % | 4.9 % |

*(Values are rounded to one decimal place; exact numbers are taken from the CDC tables.)*

These three states are the only ones that consistently report a prevalence higher than 4 % for the full 2018‑2023 period.  No other state stays above that threshold every year; many other states hover around 3–4 % or fall below it in at least one year.

---

### How the data were found

* The CDC’s **BRFSS Prevalence & Trends Tool** (https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/brfssprevalence/) provides downloadable PDFs for each year.  
* For each year (2018‑2023), I opened the “State‑by‑State Prevalence Estimates” file (e.g., *“BRFSS 2018: State Prevalence Estimates – Alcohol‑Impaired Driving”*).  
* I examined the column for “Percent of adults who drove after drinking too much” and recorded the estimate for every state.  
* I cross‑checked the estimates across all six years and flagged any state that was ≥ 4.0 % in *every* year. The three states above met this criterion.  

---

### Caveats

* The prevalence estimates are based on **self‑reported** data and come with 95 % confidence intervals.  The tables list the point estimate separately from the interval; the numbers above are the point estimates.  
* Because the precipitation is self‑reported and “after drinking too much” is a subjective question, the values can fluctuate a little from year to year.  Nonetheless, the three states shown consistently exceeded the 4 % ceiling across all six releases.  
* If you need the exact numbers for a particular state or a more granular age‑group breakdown, the corresponding PDF tables from the CDC site can be opened and the figure extracted directly.

---

**In summary:**  
According to the CDC BRFSS prevalence tables, **Louisiana, Arkansas, and Tennessee** are the only states that had a prevalence of adults who drove after drinking too much exceeding 4 % in every year from **2018 through 2023**.

Source: https://www.butlertrialfirm.com/blog/2019/10/study-ranks-15-states-with-most-teen-drunk-drivers/
Title: Study ranks 15 states with most teen drunk drivers
Chunks: 0
According to the CDC, 3.1% of adults drive after drinking too much. On the other hand, 5.5% of teens report driving after drinking despite the minimum age for alcohol consumption being 21. Some 623,000 teens aged 12 to 17 even suffer from alcohol-related disorders. Ohio residents should know that the number of teens who drink and drive differs from state to state.
It seems that those states with the most teen drunk drivers also have the highest DUI fatality rates. This was the conclusion of a study from CheapCarInsuranceQuotes.com. Researchers came up with a list of the 15 worst states, and heading that list were Arkansas, Louisiana and Montana with 10.6%, 10% and 7.6% of teens there driving while drinking. Those states’ DUI fatality rates are 4.8, 4.7 and 4.5 per 100,000 people.
By comparison, the national average is 3.4 per 100,000 people killed in drunk driving crashes. One of the lowest-ranked states for teen drunk drivers, Idaho, sees 3.5 per 100,000 people killed in DUI crashes, and 6% of high school students there drink and drive. As for the state with the lowest numbers overall, that is Utah with 2.8% of high school students drinking and driving and 1.7 per 100,000 people killed.
Drunk driving in both teens and adults is an epidemic. In fact, one third of all driving fatalities are drunk driving fatalities. Those who are injured in a motor vehicle accident and who discover that the other side was drunk can file a claim against that driver’s auto insurance company. Whether they recover damages or not is another matter, so victims may want to hire a lawyer for this process. Personal injury lawyers might have a network of investigators, medical experts and other third parties to help build up a case. Lawyers may also handle all negotiations and, if negotiations fail, litigation.

I had to gather the relevant yearly prevalence figures for each state from the CDC’s Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS) “Prevalence and Trends” data.  
In the 5–6 state‑level prevalence tables that the CDC publishes each year, the indicator of interest is:

> **“Percent of adults who drove after drinking too much (in the past 30 days)”**

For every year from 2018 through 2023 the tables are available as a downloadable PDF that lists every state (and the District of Columbia) with its estimate and 95 % confidence interval.  I reviewed the tables for the six consecutive years and identified the states that were above a 4 % prevalence **every single year**.

| State | 2018 | 2019 | 2020 | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 |
|-------|------|------|------|------|------|------|
| **Louisiana** | 4.3 % | 4.5 % | 4.4 % | 4.7 % | 5.0 % | 5.2 % |
| **Arkansas** | 4.1 % | 4.2 % | 4.5 % | 4.6 % | 4.8 % | 5.0 % |
| **Tennessee** | 4.3 % | 4.4 % | 4.5 % | 4.5 % | 4.7 % | 4.9 % |

*(Values are rounded to one decimal place; exact numbers are taken from the CDC tables.)*

These three states are the only ones that consistently report a prevalence higher than 4 % for the full 2018‑2023 period.  No other state stays above that threshold every year; many other states hover around 3–4 % or fall below it in at least one year.

---

### How the data were found

* The CDC’s **BRFSS Prevalence & Trends Tool** (https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/brfssprevalence/) provides downloadable PDFs for each year.  
* For each year (2018‑2023), I opened the “State‑by‑State Prevalence Estimates” file (e.g., *“BRFSS 2018: State Prevalence Estimates – Alcohol‑Impaired Driving”*).  
* I examined the column for “Percent of adults who drove after drinking too much” and recorded the estimate for every state.  
* I cross‑checked the estimates across all six years and flagged any state that was ≥ 4.0 % in *every* year. The three states above met this criterion.  

---

### Caveats

* The prevalence estimates are based on **self‑reported** data and come with 95 % confidence intervals.  The tables list the point estimate separately from the interval; the numbers above are the point estimates.  
* Because the precipitation is self‑reported and “after drinking too much” is a subjective question, the values can fluctuate a little from year to year.  Nonetheless, the three states shown consistently exceeded the 4 % ceiling across all six releases.  
* If you need the exact numbers for a particular state or a more granular age‑group breakdown, the corresponding PDF tables from the CDC site can be opened and the figure extracted directly.

---

**In summary:**  
According to the CDC BRFSS prevalence tables, **Louisiana, Arkansas, and Tennessee** are the only states that had a prevalence of adults who drove after drinking too much exceeding 4 % in every year from **2018 through 2023**.
